title: Summarise twelve orders by country
prompt: `orders` holds twelve rows from the messy export, and the country names have inconsistent capitals. Build `revenue_by_country`, a dictionary from cleaned country name (use `.strip().title()`) to the sum of `total`. Build `large_ids`, a list of the `order_id`s whose total is 60 or more, in their original order. Set `web_count` to the number of orders whose channel is exactly `"web"`.
hints: Loop over `orders` once for the dictionary: clean the country into a variable first, then update the total for that key.
`revenue_by_country[country] = revenue_by_country.get(country, 0) + order["total"]` adds to an existing total or starts a new one.
`large_ids = [o["order_id"] for o in orders if o["total"] >= 60]`. For `web_count`, `sum(1 for o in orders if o["channel"] == "web")` or a loop with `+= 1` both work.
explanation: Cleaning the key before using it is what makes `"united kingdom"`, `"UNITED KINGDOM"` and `"United Kingdom"` land in the same bucket; without it you would get three UK entries and a total split three ways. The `.get(key, 0)` pattern handles the first appearance of each country. The comprehension keeps the list in the original order because it walks `orders` front to back. The grand total across countries is still 854.0, which is a quick way to confirm that grouping neither lost nor double-counted a row: always check that the parts add up to the whole.

checks.countries-clean: Exactly six cleaned country names, with no case variants
checks.all-revenue: The country totals add up to 854.0, the sum of all twelve orders
